summary: Surveys deployed and experimental in-network storage systems and discusses how they apply to the DECADE architecture, which separates application data storage from the applications themselves. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine lockers in the middle of the internet where anything can drop off or pick up files. This looks at how existing locker-like systems work and whether they fit one design.

subtitle: Surveying existing storage systems that can be deployed in the network to help applications manage content.

tldr.problem: Networks face growing traffic from content distribution, and applications need better ways to manage and store data in the network itself. The DECADE architecture proposes letting applications use provider-based storage within the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys existing and experimental in-network storage systems including CDNs, P2P caches, cloud services, and novel approaches like Named Data Networking. It describes how each system handles data access, management, search, access control, and resource control.
tldr.outcome: The survey provides a comprehensive reference for understanding storage technologies available or proposed for the internet, and identifies which capabilities are essential for DECADE. It helped guide the development of a standard way for applications to use in-network storage.

today: RFC 6392 is an Informational RFC that provides a comprehensive baseline for understanding in-network storage approaches as of 2011. While it does not define a protocol, it influenced the development of DECADE and other storage-related standards. The systems and approaches it describes remain relevant reference points for network architects designing content delivery and storage solutions.

sections.title: The DECADE Vision for In-Network Storage
sections.content:
DECADE (DECoupled Application Data Enroute) is an architecture that lets applications store data in dedicated storage devices placed inside the network, managed by network providers. Unlike traditional content caches that network operators control completely, DECADE allows applications themselves to manage access to their stored content and control resource usage.

The driving force behind DECADE is the dramatic increase in storage capacity and decrease in storage cost over the past two decades. This makes it practical to deploy large storage systems throughout the network. A key motivator is P2P applications, which can upload through network storage instead of using last-mile bandwidth, reducing the load on ISP networks. However, DECADE could benefit many other applications as well.

This survey examines deployed and experimental in-network storage systems to evaluate their suitability for DECADE and document the design space.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet storage lets programs save files at computers spread around the network. DECADE wants apps to control their own storage without the network running it for them.

sections.title: Components of In-Network Storage Systems
sections.content:
All in-network storage systems share common functions that the survey uses to compare them. The Data Access Interface is how users read and write data—some systems offer both operations, some only reads.

The Data Management Operations let users control their stored content, such as deleting or moving files. A Data Search Capability lets users find what they have stored. Access Control Authorization determines who can read or write: public-unrestricted (anyone), public-restricted (selected networks or users without credentials), or private (credentials required).

The Resource Control Interface lets applications manage how much bandwidth or connections their storage operations consume. The Discovery Mechanism helps users find where storage is located. Finally, Storage Mode describes how data is organized: as a file system (hierarchical), as objects (independent data chunks), or as raw blocks (like a disk).
sections.plainLanguage: Storage systems have different ways to store things, who can access them, and how you find them. Some work like a filing cabinet you control, others like a library where the librarian decides access.

sections.title: Deployed and Experimental Storage Systems
sections.content:
The survey covers 15 systems across deployed and experimental categories. Amazon S3 is a widely deployed cloud storage service using HTTP, with strong authorization using signed queries. CDNs like Akamai are massively deployed for static content delivery through edge servers worldwide, but give clients only read access.

BranchCache (enterprise cache for branch offices) and P2P caches are transparent systems that intercept traffic and cache it locally. Web caches and photo-sharing sites like Flickr offer user-facing storage. OceanStore is a resilient distributed system using Byzantine agreement. Delay-Tolerant Networks use persistent storage on nodes for long-disruption scenarios.

More experimental approaches include Named Data Networking (NDN), which names data instead of hosts and caches by name at routers; Network of Information (NetInf), which treats information objects as primary architectural elements; Cache-and-Forward (CNF), which uses storage-rich routers; Network Traffic Redundancy Elimination (RE), which stores data patterns to compress repeated traffic; and CDMI (Cloud Data Management Interface), a standard for accessing cloud storage.
sections.plainLanguage: Many storage systems already exist—some for companies to share files (S3), some for videos to load fast (CDNs), some experimental ones that store data by content name instead of location.

sections.title: Key Findings About Storage Capabilities
sections.content:
The survey reveals several important observations about existing systems. Deployed systems like Amazon S3 and CDNs excel at scale and business relationships but often lock users into specific models. Transparent caches (P2P caches, BranchCache) require no changes to applications but give applications no control—the network operator decides what is cached and for how long.

Experimental information-centric approaches (NDN, NetInf) would require fundamental changes to Internet routing and would place storage on routers everywhere, not in dedicated devices. Some systems lack critical capabilities: many have no data management operations, search capabilities, or resource control interfaces. Most systems do not allow applications to explicitly control which content is stored, when it is removed, or how bandwidth is allocated.

The survey identifies that no existing deployed system fully meets DECADE requirements. DECADE needs application-level control of storage, explicit resource management, and the ability to work across multiple administrative domains while maintaining security.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems let you control your files, but they are limited. Others cache things automatically, but you have no say. Most miss some feature DECADE needs.

sections.title: Storage-Related Protocols and Standards
sections.content:
Beyond complete storage systems, the RFC examines protocols and interfaces relevant to in-network storage. HTTP is used by many storage systems as the access protocol. iSCSI provides block-level storage access over IP. NFS (Network File System) is a long-established file system protocol. OAuth provides authorization delegation for web services. WebDAV extends HTTP with file management operations.

These protocols and standards represent mature, proven approaches to storage access, authorization, and management. The survey notes that DECADE protocols should leverage existing IETF standards where possible, and that careful protocol choices will be important for DECADE's success.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols already exist for storing data and managing access on the network. These could be used as building blocks for DECADE.
